Have to hand it to them, thought Murray (et al.) would just cut their losses and fade into obscurity, but they swallowed their pride and made the game half decent, and while I shant avoid the fact it was once an overhyped dissapointment (although the jury's still out on how much of that was actually Sony's fault) I buried the hatchet about 1 hour in when I started planet hopping with friends.

Pros:
+ Massive universe filled with diverse (albeit one trick pony) planets with at least one that'll appeal to someone. For me it was a planet covered in fractalizing hexagons.
+ Good fun with friends thanks to a solid multiplayer experience. Players can roam freely and aren't tied to each other in order to do things, you and your bro can go mining on a radioactive hellhole while your mate becomes an interplanetary used ship salesman and your buddy ol' pal can go command a space freighter, it's great. 
+ The full crafting-survival package from scavenging to base building in a fittingly massive sandbox.
+ A good choice of spaceships and weapons with the appeal of loot chest style randomness that draws people to Borderlands or Diablo and makes it quite exciting to visit a new solar system in hopes of finding something awesome.
+ A nice, vast, atmospheric soundtrack perfect for exploring a vast universe. Compliments to 65daysofstatic! 
+ A good deal of content that's perfect for those looking for their next time sink game.

Cons: More often than not nitpicks but they're so ubiquitous that they'll end up testing your patience
- Gameplay is very laidback, with sci-fi thrills being awfully few and far between. 
- Planets can be awfully boring, everything is a sweeping hilly plain with the occasional cave, hill or water feature. The only thing that differs are the props that dot the landscape, as a result playing alone can become hauntingly lonely and the environments become boring after a while. I woudn't mind if they added some more geographical features like waterfalls.
- Gunplay feels loose and anemic, how can a sci-fi shotgun lack such impact? Why is my rifle being wielded like a pistol?
- Very slow start plus hazardous weather starting planet equals frustrating game when you're forced to huddle into your spaceship every 2-4 minutes as it gets hard to manage your sodium intake both in-game and irl. I would honestly suggest more serene starting planets with the more inhospitable planets introduced later in the game.
- There is not one planet I've found in my playtime that had just nice, non-life threatening weather conditions, even the paradise looking planets had the occasional superheated rainstorm.
- The common "Sentinel" enemies are a constant nuisance with no means for the player to repel them or create a safe space for mining and crafting, often leading to a game of grandma's footsteps with floating drones when you're trying to mine for important resources otherwise the space police will come to melt your face off for great justice.

Overall I'd recommend this game, Hello Games really saved this game from the scrapheap (earning my respect in the process) and if you're looking for a relaxed space adventure in a vast universe I'd give this one a try, especially if you can find some friends to tag along.

I've stopped playing video games for quite awhile due to being unimpressed and uninterested with most of the new titles, preferring to watch the interesting ones played by streamers instead of participating, I'm also not a fan of sci-fi and sandbox games but NMS is an exception to both of those statements--it's truly a wonderful game and the developers made one of the most epic comeback which I've only seen happen with FF14 (but let's be real, Hello Games comeback is more impressive considering the size of their team compared to the colossal FF14 team). 

I've recently just bought the game but I've been watching its subreddit and community so I'm quite aware of how terrible the game was at launch. I'm someone who's not big on sci-fi and sandbox games so it's entirely up to you whether or not to consider my ramblings.



[b]THINGS I LIKED ABOUT THE GAME[/b]

- Singleplayer experience and modding scene
- Optional multiplayer experience if you wish to play with your friends and other fellows
- The alluring palette and color of the worlds, or 'aesthetic' as one would put it
- Starships, freighters and exocrafts
- Planetary explorations
- Basebuilding
- Multitude of planets to explore
- Procedural generation
- Very chill game, there's a 'Creative Mode' if you only wish to indulge yourself in exploration and creativity
- PvP is [u]not[/u] a core feature of the game, it's just a side distraction and has very little impact and unrewarding. The game is more of a co-op experience than anything else. I just want to explore freely in games like these, but I have no qualms of having PvP incentivized either.
- And of course, the developers, Hello Games




[b]THINGS I DIDN'T LIKE ABOUT THE GAME[/b]

- [u]The occasional crashes[/u]. The crashes are not about rigs, it's very evident in the the discussion board where tons of people with even monster rigs crash. The crashes are very random, sometimes I crash within 3 minutes of playing and sometimes I can play for hours without any freezing and crashing.
- [u]The limited palette[/u]. I also listed the game's 'aesthetic' as a positive point but after quite a lot of planet hopping, I've noticed that the 'color' of planets often look similar (similar skies, similar ocean, no variants), it lacks variety of flavor.
- [u]The lack of variance leads to making the game feel 'small'[/u]. High chances that the next planet you'll explore looks very similar to the ones you've already seen. The generation area is very small that you'll see the same terrain in a few kilometers with just [i]very slight[/i] difference so there's no real reason to explore further just to see a [i]slightly[/i] taller hill.
- [u]No reason to explore further[/u]. This is not an epic action or combat game (although you can get occasional doses of combat with sentinel or pirate battles, if you're in the mood -- or avoid them if you're not in the mood).

The gameplay loop is fairly straightforward -- land on a planet, explore around, find resources and other cool toys to upgrade your inventory and your equipment, rinse and repeat.  But the primary draw of the game (for me at least) is not the gameplay itself, but the exploration aspect, or just wandering around enjoying the scenery and the weird and wonderful critters that you find on each world.

The game has received quite a few updates over the years, with the NEXT update and the Abyss update in particular dramatically expanding the exploration possibilities, and giving you more reasons to stay and explore a single world for longer rather than just jumping worlds as soon as you've gathered enough resources to refuel your ship.

This is a great "chill-out" game, where you just want something to kick back, relax, and have fun wandering around without pressure -- or blast some pirates if you're in that mood.

And the space combat doesn't suck (unlike many other games that feature it) -- at least once you disable the default tethered mode.

Didn't jump on the NmS train when it first came out due to all the backslash (for devs lies etc..).

Now I can't suggest it more.
The devs outdid themselves with an apparently endless stream of (monthly) updates that really push this title on the right direction.

The game itself is heavily focused on two elements: exploration and building.
You are free to roam in a procedural generated galaxy where each planet in each system is different.
You can name all the flora/fauna you discover as well as all the unexplored planets you find.
Biomes vary a lot among different planets, albeit they are the same within a single planet.

On the building side you can build your base on any point (even underwater) of any planet.
Each base can be built in a custom using different unlockable components and decorations as building blocks.
Each base can be interconnected through multiple buildable portals.
You can also unlock a freighter to use as mobile base for your journey.

The procedural generated ships design, the presence of landing vehicles helps to complete the experience.

The feeling is like a sort of starbound in 3d, albeit more polished, varied, and constantly updated.

I pre-ordered this game in 2016 before it came out, and like most, was greatly let down when the vast over-marketing of the game became apparent. I tried to request a refund for the game but had more than two hours (two hours which were spent loading into the first planet several times) so I couldn't. I was angry my $60 had been wasted on a glaringly unfinished game. Over time, I got over my lost money, and eventually, all but forgot about the game.

Today, I'm immensely glad I didn't get to refund it, because just a week ago I thought to myself "You know what? This game's probably changed quite a bit in two years. I have nothing better to do, so I'll give it a second go." In seven days I put almost 70 hours into this game. Why? A better question is "Where do I even start?"

The atmosphere. With truly beautiful planets and awe-inspiring views in space, the visual experience is memorable. But on top of that you have the mystery of the story and its characters, further combined with the experiences you make in your endeavours to explore lush, harsh, or barren planets that could either be brimming with strange, beautiful plants and animals, or be totally void of life altogether. And not to mention, the *stunning* soundtrack No Man's Sky brings to its audience. The music always casts overtones of fitting moods, feelings of wonder, joy, paranoia, creepiness, vastness, or, at its most smile-delivering moments, quiet peace.

The universe. No Man's Sky holds within the resolution of your monitor a literally infinite realm of solar systems, primitive lifeforms, alien encounters, soaring starships, imposing fleets, dusty highlands, shadowed forests, hazy sunrises, and sinister robots. I could go on with the list, as there's vast experiences to be had in the game, but I'm sure a few people are already wondering when this review is going to end.

And finally, the story. I hadn't even known there *was* a story to the game, or at least not beyond the mystery of the Atlas stations. And you can definitely play the game without investing into the story missions much and go for pure gameplay, it's certainly built for both kinds of people. But 70 hours later, I admit it, I have been blown away by the story this game has told. I'm not even done with it yet, that's how compelled I am to write this review. I won't spoil anything of course, but the captivatingly-deep story, with its dream-like surreality and its varied and unique host of characters create a story worthy of a novel. It starts off as the expected story of "What is this place and how did I get here?" and quickly progresses to a cosmic tale of four races, god-like machines, souls lost between time and space, and searching for a greater purpose and a tangible meaning to reality. There are some clear influences from science fiction already told, such as authors like Asimov, movies like Star Wars, and I even caught a System Shock reference, which made me pause for a moment to laugh in an otherwise serious and important scene. No Man's Sky seems to take almost every fantasy from science fiction of the past, like being stranded on a remote, alien world, meeting various citizens of the galaxy of races big and small, machines that have accumulated galaxy-wide power, and leading a fleet of fantastic starships from the bridge of your grand flagship, and sew them together into an masterfully-conceived game that, in my opinion, has arguably out-done many of its similar predecessors with its immersion, gameplay, and story that until now were never able to grab my imagination so strongly. 

I am grateful that Sean Murray took the initial explosive backlash from the over-zealous mistake of calling 2016 a full release, and still went on with his creation to thoroughly flesh it out and make his ideas come to life, still holding on and turning a scary, too-soon release into two years' product of dedication.

While I would like to conclude and let you get on with your life and take a nap after reading through this seemingly unending review, it would be wrong to end it there on reveling and glee, and not address the fact that the game still isn't done. That's obvious, from both the continuing roadmap and the number of bugs continuing to harass players. There are also a fair number of things in the game that struck me as lacking, or just needing to be expanded upon. It does get repetitive to see another Gek in another minor settlement asking you to take another set of scans on another set of creatures, and after a while the starships, frigates, and to some extent the freighters start to seem like the same couple of small fleets are following you to each system, and it *definitely* got very annoying very fast to get assaulted by a dinky little Sentinel drone every time I tried mining a rock within thirty feet of it. (however that is supposed to be overbearing, the plot expands much upon it)
That said, the game is still in development. There isn't exactly a legion of Bethesda development teams cranking away on the game, it's definitely a small-scale team; a small-scale team working on a *very* ambitious game. So, it is to be expected that there are a good few bugs and glitches and what-just-happened moments, as well as areas of gameplay that feel kind of underwhelming. Anyone who decides to pay for a game that's undergoing this level of construction has to be aware of and prepared to meet some frustrating moments. And of course, over time, especially with such a dedicated group of people, the bugs will be ironed out, the flimsier features will be given more depth, and the functionality of the game will be smoothed out. 

But yes, I am here as a lover of games big and small and famous and obscure to tell you that despite the infamous disaster of a release, despite the definite bugs and empty moments of a game still in active development, and despite the forbidding "Mixed reviews" status it has on the Store, this is a game that delivers to those who stick with it. As I said, I'm not even finished with the main story and this game has already given me thrills and chills. When the day comes that Murray dusts off his hands and the team wipes the sweat from their collective brow, No Man's Sky will have become a true work of art, one that will make a special place in the right players' hearts.

Alright, I'm done. Thanks for reading this.

Having been a long time player of Elite, I was eager to get my hands on No Man's Sky from the point of the NEXT update in order to see what I'd been missing. I'd say that No Man's Sky is more Minecraft than Elite Dangerous, in fact having a candy cane look to the game and atmosphere that takes it away from being a simulation and more puts it in the realm of eye candy. 

The palette is actually quite nice, but does give it a bit of a surreal atmosphere akin to old school video games.

The graphics are very nice and despite running the game on an old LGA775 quad core system Win10x64 8GB ram, after much tweaking I was able to get an appreciable frame rate. Not a great framerate but certainly good enough to play without sacrificing the graphics setings too much.

The music and audio are great, bringing atmospheric tunes to the background during exploration and grinding (to collect crafting resources).

The story slowly unfolds as you make progress throughout the universe. I haven't been any further than my starting system yet, so I've not seen much. I've heard there's a lot of variety to see in the game in terms of randomly generated scenery and the life forms that populate the various planets.

This game is not the Elite killer for certain, for it is completely a different experience altogether. The only similarity is that it takes place in a futuristic science fiction open world. In fact the two games complement different kinds of gameplay and quell very different cravings for challenge in such experiences. There are Elite days, and there are NMS days and for every player they'll be different.

Pros
+ Good graphics though the palette is a bit like candy. Candy is good, but too much can give you a sugar hangover.
+ Gameplay is good though sometimes dealing with hostile lifeforms and drones on planets can be frustrating. You'll be making a few trips to your last death position to collect the loot from your prior life.
+ Variety is certainly at play here and there are many things to discover and see including scenery, lifeforms and mysteries.
+ Its difficult to sum up the quality of a piece of work that a small team have literally put a decade of their life into crafting. While playing, you're going to encounter a lot of their creativity and craftiness but chances are no amount of words can sum that up here. You've got to play it for yourself.
+ Random variety seems to be shaped in such a way that makes sense. For instance, you won't see fish with legs too often. Most of the evolutionary traits of creatures makes exploration rewarding. Sometimes its just fun to stand back and watch the ecosystems in action.


Cons
- Demanding in terms of hardware. Tweakable but still demanding which can be frustrating if you're dealing with hostile species or drones while grinding for crafting resources.
- Planetary in atmosphere flight is a little dodgy and difficult as well. Don't expect yourself to be a flying ace with how the ship(s) are controlled. A stable yaw control with hovering would be nice and make collecting your lost crafting resources much easier and less frustrating. Being able to control your ship like a helicopter while in the atmosphere would be a big improvement.

Overall, the game at its current state (Abyss Update) is well worth the asking price of $60 CDN given the variety of features and content, though I fortunately managed to get it on sale and if you see it on sale, don't miss the opportunity. 

I've never played this during its earlier incarnations so I'm not going to comment on that issue. I recommend this game, but not as an alternative to Elite Dangerous because its completely a different kind of game.

No Man's Sky was a game that, despite all the criticism and controversy, continued to be updated and improved on. The NEXT/Abyss Updates have made this game enjoyable, though it is still very grindy.

First off, I'd like to mention that I really like space exploration games, especially playing with friends and being able to build bases. This game, however, is not for everyone. If you like games that tell you what to do, this is not for you. Often times, you'll probably find yourself really bored as the game's campaign is probably one of its biggest downsides.

The graphics are clean and the planets you find range from beautiful and Earth-like to radioactive. There's a good mix of different environments, though most of the planets you find you probably will skip. The performance, however, is troubling. Even running this on an RX 580 8GB, I'm barely hitting 40-50 FPS at lowest settings 1080p. Nvidia cards seem to be much better optimized, but I'd still like to see better performance for us Radeon users.

The campaign is very mediocre. While I haven't finished it yet (or delved too deep), it mostly consisted of you visiting a spot, talking to someone, going somewhere else, etc. There isn't any really exciting part to it. Luckily, the game gets over this with its planetary exploration system. When you find a lush planet and land on it for the first time, you'll be swept with a feeling of accomplishment and wonder. Furthermore, the base-building is also adequate. The types of rooms you can construct are varied, and with the Abyss update you can even go underwater. The worst part of the game is, in my opinion, how grindy it is. While I've heard that this can be fixed in the late-game, so far, mining with a laser beam is just boring. If the devs could make the game less focused on grind and more focused on action, this game would be a far lot better

Overall, No Man's Sky is a game that does a lot of things right, but is still unpolished. For $60, I wouldn't recommend it unless you love these type of games, but for the price I got it ($26), I will recommend it. I have faith in Hello Games to keep improving this game, and hope I'm correct.

Peaceful, relaxing, and sometimes thrilling. 

I've always found No Man's Sky to be an enjoyable little pass-time, even before the NEXT update. That update just made the game feel more whole and complete. There's a certain charm about the game that makes it feel very unique. It's not trying to make itself out to be another game, and yet it provides experiences that feel so familiar. It's not the best game out there, without a doubt, but it is definitely unique.

It definitely comes down to being a game that exists for those who do not only expect every game to have some kind of 'meta', or aspire to be an AAA title with explosive stories and the most viciously perilous combat, providing you with reasons to brag to others. Everything feels so relaxed—it's quite 'dreamy'. And, I like that. A lot, actually. It allows you to just take a few steps back and enjoy a game without the rush of searching for an 'end game', enabling you to just enjoy it for what it is—an exploration game. 

There is a lot that repeats itself, and certain things do become quite tedious and boring fast, mind you. One instance of what I'm talking about is the NPCs. They are far from the most expansive in terms of dialogue. It would be awesome to see that expanded on, so that you don't feel like every system you visit is the same. However, looking past that, and the repetitive nature of the game, it honestly does makes up for what it lacks with the sheer beauty of its worlds; the creatures that exists within those words, and it's gorgeous soundtrack. Are there a lot of things that I wish would be implemented, or bugs that I'd like to see fixed? Of course, there's always going to be a lot of details that need polishing up. What's this game about? I can sum up what the entire game is about, in one word: Storage.

You start on a planet and you need to repair your ship, in order to do so you need materials, so you set about collecting materials and put them in your tiny backpack but you also need materials to fuel your life support, refuel your ship, and so on, so your biggest initial concern is: storage.

Eventually you'll want to leave that planet and set off to find new planets, but in order to do so, you'll need hyperfuel and a better jump drive. In order to build these things you'll need even more materials, so that's right you'll need storage.

Thankfully there's a multitude of POIs on the surface of planets that you can find and, after collecting the proper materials, build more storage, one slot at a time. There's also a million other ships in the universe that you can buy, they're all pretty much the same, but you'll end up going with whichever one you can find that gives you the most storage.

Eventually you can buy a Freighter, no you can't fight enemy fleets with it or conquer the galaxy, it's mostly just there to help you store things. A neat feature is the ability to house an entire fleet of 6 little ships onboard, where you can store more items.

You can also build bases on planets, why would you do this? No, not to defend yourself or conduct research or dominate territory, those bases are mostly there to help you store things. A nice feature is the ground vehicles you can build, it's still much much faster to travel around on a planet in your tiny ship, but the ground vehicles have an inventory that provides some extra storage.

Sometimes pirates will detect the valuable items in your storage, and one or two will spawn that you'll have to defeat in a relaxing little mini-game called space-ship auto-aim whack-a-mole. Careful not to collect things near drones, they don't like it when you store things and will attack you, no you can't fight back they'll just infinitely respawn and follow you to space if you try to leave. Better just run away. Yes there are weapons, but they are entirely pointless so you shouldn't carry any, it's best to devote that space for storage.

My "technical" review of the game will be at the end, first i want to address the evolution of NMS and Hello Games.
 
Ok, so now that the game is much closer to what people expected from it, i feel it's a good time for a review.
With the NEXT update, Hello Games showed that they could bring the game most people wanted since the first trailers. But with it came a promise to keep the game growing, and since then the updates have been non-stop. From the community events, Abyss, and now the Visions update, which caters to what people are still asking, more variation in biomes, more alien-y stuff, and always trying to keep bugs in check (colossal task given the procedural generation nature and scope/size of the game). I truly think that HG deserves not only our forgiveness but also our admiration, for sticking to their love-child instead of running with the money.

I liked the game from day one. It was the first game i preordered, and i didn't feel cheated, even though i knew all the features that had been left out. I was very impressed by the technical aspect of a huge universe that is procedurally created, and not randomized, and i think it's something that will be very explored in the future( EA tried it with Mass Effect Andromeda and failed, and when comparing a company like EA to Hello Games makes it clear to me that Sean and his team are geniuses, at least in coding and visual/sound desing). In terms of coding and programming it was masterfully done, even with all the bugs and performance issues, it still worked very well, and i felt the sense of awe and wonder that i think Sean wanted us to see and feel. 

But gameplay-wise, the game was lacking. I was happy just finding cool looking planets and solar systems and going wild with photo mode, but obviously, that wouldn't be enough to keep the game afloat. Then came the backlash of users, so frustrated with what they had been promised and that wasn't in the game at all. It was very well deserved, and in fact, it had a big role in the way the game has been shaped. With every update, the game kept getting better, and with NEXT, the game is so much closer to, not only what Sean envisioned, but also to what gamers wanted. Hello Games listened to the fans, and that is not only commendable, but it should also serve as a lesson to other companies, big and small, out there.

So with that out of the way, here's my review of the No Mans Sky:

Visuals and Graphics -
  The game is gorgeous and very different, with a very stylized and non-realistic design. The procedural nature of the engine makes it so that you can find the most lush and colourful planets, or the most desolate and barren landscape ever, with every possible variation in between. Right now as of NEXT, the game is much more optimized than at launch and the graphics are even better than at launch. That said, you still need a somewhat beefy PC to run it properly, as in some planets where, for example, the weather is harsh, and there are a lot of particles and a lot of assets being generated and drawn, the frames will dip a lot when compared to when you are in space or in emptier planets. There is still room for some optimization, but i think HG are doing a great job with it so far.

 Sound Design and Music - 
  The idea of a procedural sond design is a lot trickier than it might seem. All the sounds of creatures are also generated, and it's by far a lot harder to provide variety in sound than in graphics. Still the game sounds incredible, and you have the weirdest alien-y sounds to more familiar tech and machinery sounds, all very well done and fitting the context. The music is done by the band 65 Days of Static, and they achieved a great balance between making awe-inspiring music, scarier and more alien sounding music, all the while keeping the game sounding futuristic, misterious, beautiful and engaging. And again, the music is also procedurally generated, mixing different instruments and parts with a gigantic number of possible combinations, wich means you will never hear the same song twice. That is an amazing achievement by itself.

Gameplay - 
  So, in here lies the question whether this game is for you or not. The gameplay is varied, but might feel a bit of a grind for some people. There are modes for all tastes besides the Normal. You can choose Creative mode, if you don't want to search for the resources and just want to build and/or explore. You can also go for Survival or Permadeath if you're into harcore suvival. The gameplay has 4 pillars, Survival (encompasses finding resources to build better equipment and evolve your character/base/ship/freighter and fleet), Exploration (finding planets and systems with better and more rare resources), Combat ( fighting on the ground with a blaster, hunting creatures or The Sentinels, dogfights in space with your ship, or sending your freighter/fleet on missions) and Trading (everything in the game is "buyable" and "sellable", be it resources, the stuff you build, ships and freighters, you name it.)


With the promise of future updates focusing on the community, weekly events, and the online component, all beeing free, with no microtransactions in sight, the game should only get better and more entertaining, and for all that i totally recommend it, especially if you get it on sale. If you do, and want someone to play it with, feel free to add me on Steam. :)

Thank you for reading, and leave some input in the comments if you want to, and props to Hello Games for the game, and for sticking with the community in creating No Mans Sky.

While this game didn't have the most impressive launch, I've always felt it was a unique and entertaining piece of software.  It wasn't what people expected, the hype train was far too massively built up for that, and it probably launched at least a year or more too early.  That said, on launch I still got 30ish hours out of it, and enjoyed my time with it then.

Over the past year, each of the previous two patches brought me back (about ~10 hours each time) and added new depth to the game to make it worth checking out all over again.  Building bases, driving around in vehicles, owning freighters were all very nice additions to broaden the game, but at its core it was still a walking simulator, a trip from point A to point B and to enjoy the sights in between.

The 1.3 update just deepened that and with 30 hours of story, trading, missions, portals, and tons of other new features this feels like a new game almost (or at least a very impressive expansion pack).  I am excited for the future of this game, almost more-so than I was before launch.

I was going to write a review when the game launched, but felt that it wasn't a finished product and while I enjoyed it then, it wasn't something I felt good about recommending to anyone else.  The 1.1 and 1.2 updates while adding to it, still didn't make me feel satisfied enough to recommend it.  The 1.3 to me, is more than enough now for me to give this game a good recommendation.  The core of the game is still there... enjoy the journey, but now there is a lot of depth to explore in that journey.

The continued updates to this game make it closer and closer to the original dream that so many had of what it could be.

Big props to Hello Games for the continued (free) support and development of this game long after the point when many other developers would have kicked it to the curb (or at the very least sold the updates as DLCs).  That said, if they ever do decide to do a paid DLC, expansion, or sequel, I would gladly thrown down the cash.

UPDATE 09/20/2017

Since my PC can't run this game properly, I got it on PS4 and I'm capable of giving a better insight about it.
I stay on my ground and say that this game is still something that not everyone can enjoy. However, I must admit that after the 1.3 Update the game got a HECK of a lot better.

First of all, missions. These are not necessary to play and they can be pretty repetitive. However, these can be useful when you need some money, technologies and other stuff. Not counting small boosts for your reputation.

The renewed interface simplifies a lot of things, like keeping track of progresses with a certain race or guild.

I can't judge the story content yet since I haven't finished it yet, but so far seems rather intriguing.

The amount of items that have been added is very high. They also added an option to craft the same item in one slot and upload all discoveries at once (FINALLY). You can also literally make a business in your own base by creating materials and selling them for high prices.

Despite a lot of planets still feel the same, if I have to play the part of the explorer and look for all plants, minerals, animals and waypoints, it gets satisfying (plus, it also rewards Units). However, any player would probably BEG for an option to find again the discovered waypoints on a planet (I had to give up a S rank Multi-Tool at the very beginning because I didn't have the money to buy it).

They added portals and a form of limited multiplayer, which allows people to visit other players' discovered planet and meet eachother. I didn't have a chance to experience this yet, though.

Crashed freighters are something very cool and the rewards... USED to be very worth (just 60 pieces of Iron and you'd get a good number of Units and Nanites), but since the 1.37 update, opening each vault requires some random materials and sometimes the value of such materials is much higher than the contents. For example, I encountered a crashed freighter whose vaults required a circuit board each to be opened, which are tedious to craft and can be sold for about 1 million Units each. I didn't open them yet but, looking around, currently they don't seem to be worth the effort since they net around 50.000 Units. I think this needs to be rebalanced to grant much more substantial rewards (for example about 2 million Units or 2000 Nanites in each vault requiring a circuit board).

The space combat, on the other hand, is not very enjoyable. The spaceship doesn't seem to control that well, even with a controller. While I move is very hard to hit the enemy and, most of the time I stand still in one place shooting the enemy while they shoot me back hoping my shield will hold long enough, otherwise it's time to run and wait for the shield to recharge (UPDATE: looking around, this is probably just because I have a Transport type ship, which may not be suitable for space fights).
Speaking of which, Sentinel's Interceptors are a PAIN: if you try to save a freighter from pirates and, by accident, you shoot an Interceptor, they'll instantly want you dead too and there's no way to get rid of them except by engaging them (good luck with that: they are fast, relentless and in higher number than you), dying (very likely to happen if you engage them) or find a place where you can land (god help you if you're too far away. Did I mention the Pulse Jet is disabled while fighting?)

These have been my new impressions so far. Personally, I think the game got better but it's still quite rough around some edges. However, it improved enough to make me more inclined to recommend it. But... take my words with pliers: if you don't like walking for a long time, searching for creatures, materials and a limited combat system, this game is not for you (despite, however, you can play as a criminal, attack sentinels and freighters. The choice is yours. If they can add an option to conquer Space station would be probably top, since there's currently no real reason to attack them because they take no damage and just alert Sentinels). However, if you are curious, creative (there's a creative mode giving you unlimited resources), looking for a relaxing experience rather than blood-pumping action, then by all means, give it a shot. Best served with good music or a show you already saw as background noise.

After the latest update, I decided to give my own opinion about this game. PLEASE, READ EVERYTHING.
A thing I complain about Steam is that I can't give an opinion midway, so I choose the one I think is the fairest right now.
I'll tell you immediately: I LIKE this game. But can I recommend it to other people? Eeeeeeeehhh... no. Not now at least and not at this price.
The game (if you like exploration to begin with) currently is probably like eating a lot of chocolate: you like it at first but eventually you say "that's enough".

I have to say tho that the latest update is a step in the right direction. They added the possibility to build a home and hire NPCs to make researches for you. It's not necessary however, since the purpose is to reach the center of the galaxy (universe?), so why is there? Well, it's still a choice for the player. I don't think that everyone want to reach the end as fast as they can even if... well... honestly, there's not much to do. What you do on the very first planet is exactly what you do in every planet. If you like, however, to play the role of naturalist then you've got a LOOOONG way.
But even that can get troublesome: the spaceship flies way too high and too fast. If you are like me, with medium-tier PC playing with Medium details, you'll have lots of problems seeing places of interest like ruins or bases. HOWEVER... data files suggest that vehicles might come in a future update and this will probably make things a tad easier, since going on feet takes too much time to travel.

They changed the symbols for the materials and added new ones. This is particularly useful, especially when I look for a specific material of a kind and every time I end up discovering it's not the one I'm looking for.

New game modes are a nice addition. Again, it's a choice for the player. There are people who like to explore, people who want a survival challenge and people who want to just unleash their imagination. I'm glad they are trying to reach each one of them.

They added Freighters, allowing people to have GIANT ships that can be customized and carry around much more goods. In substance, it's like a flying base. Maybe I'm stretching this too much, but adding new ships (especially this kind) could mean that space battles are coming. Might not be true, but if they decided to update the game instead of abandoning it there has to be a reason.

Another good thing made by the update is that they improved the performances. Initially the game lagged quite a bit, but now is much smoother. Not exceptional, but more bearable.

I want to believe that the reason the game has been released as is it's most likely due to time constraints (they delayed the game LOTS of times). I'm not a programmer, but I'm aware that during programming EVERYTHING can happen and ruin the work. Add deadlines and outright death threats from players in case of further delays (no kidding:

https://gamerant.com/no-mans-sky-death-threats-752/ ) and this undoubtedly would make working for a game VERY stressful and in the end you say "let's release it as is, we can't delay any more".

However, as I said, in all fairness I still cannot recommend this game to everyone due to its "unfinished" status. But I'm trustful and hoping it will get better in future update and become what the devs promised. Maybe not 100% but very close at least.

Some of the things that I've found particularly inuring:

1) The improved base-building system, which is far less restricted now, includes a plethora of new options - including underwater buildings - and is consistently being added to. The addition of trophy and flora base pieces to the community rewards vendor is nice, and has encouraged me to engage with the community events.

2) Underwater exploration has been improved considerably with the release of the Abyss expansion. The underwater exocraft is an excellent addition, and there now feels like a reason to spend time on planets with large bodies of water, instead of it essentially being large bodies of "pointless space" as it felt to me beforehand.

3)  Freighter interior and freighter base-building is now much improved, and the fleet system is a nice sideline time-sink with some good perks associated. I particularly like the ability to land on all of your owned freighters, and the fact that periodically visiting different freighters in your fleet can yield resources, etc.

4) Graphical enhancements, new biomes, new flora & fauna generation, etc, all add polish to the game that it was previously lacking, as do improvements to creature AI (though it's still fairly basic).

5) Sentinel confrontations are now much more exciting, with walkers being tougher to take down, and having a more varied arsenal.

6) Horrors are a nice addition, and it's good to see that they're being improved to tackle certain of the issues that made them incredibly easy to counter (like just camping out on top of a building). The underwater horrors are cool, and I like that there's a variety, each with different abilities. Some are still a little glitchy; I've found that the Angler fish style Horror tends to end up spawning inside land, and can't be dug out with the terrain manipulator no matter how hard you try!

Some things that need further improvement:

1) NPC interactions! This is a pet peeve for many players, and I seriously hope that we'll see an update that introduces a lot more randomly spawning NPCs, with whom you can interact in a more immersive way.

2) NPCs in bases. Whilst yes, there are NPCs you can acquire for bases, they're only really there to give you access to a few things, and then they just stand there looking pretty at their terminals. Beyond that, NPC additions to bases are still totally lacking.

3) Space-craft alteration. This is another pet peeve; relying on save-skimming for the ships that I want is repetitive, mindnumbingly tedious, and not remotely immersive. We have free character alteration (love it), and whilst I don't think ship alteration should be free, the game needs a method of re-colouring and more generally altering space-craft. I think this would probably be the most well-received addition to the game - if we ever get it, that is.

On the whole, NMS is a completely different game to what it was when it first released. Hello Games have done an excellent job of listening to players, putting out content, and generally adding polish to the game; long may it continue.

[h1]No Man's Sky Review[/h1]

 
As hyped games go, No Man's Sky might just be the king, this is partially because the premise for it was so fantastic if it could be done, it would be mind-blowing. But it was also fueled by the little content Hello Games released, gameplay videos and words spoken by Mr. Murray himself whenever asked about the game.

What also added to the hype was the fact that the game would have no early release schedule like most independently released games do these days. So with only gameplay videos and trailers showing us the most insane video play any game could have, our minds just filled whatever information we were missing and our imaginations went wild. And then the game released....

At the time of this review I've clocked almost 60 hours into this game. I felt that playing it only a few hours and reviewing it would be unfair considering the sheer size of the universe within the game and amount of content the game is sure to have.

So now I will talk a little bit about the game as I see it, and talk about what I think has gone wrong, and at the end give you my score. For the purposes of this review I'm going to ignore any crashes, or bugs I encountered. Although these can be a problem, they should not used to determine the score of a game that should only be determined based on the content it has.


[u]Gameplay[/u]

For the most part the game is fairly easy. The only difficult parts I have encountered were in battles with pirates above a planet in orbit. It is important to realize that the difficulty even there was determined by two factors, 1) The amount of time one has to equip his spaceship, 2) issues with targeting said pirates. Due to a technical issue with my ship's cannons I found myself unable to damage the pirates at one point. Of course I will ignore this in giving my score but its important to understanding the difficulty of gameplay. Once this issue resolved itself, they were not terribly difficult to hit. So what then remains is the upgrades one has on the ship, not enough shields, weaker weapons, and those pirates become harder. Equally true, if you buy upgrades, they become easier.

Although the game is about exploration of the universe you are in, this quickly becomes tedious once you realize that from planet to planet, although the names of things change, the colors, and sometimes the shapes, for the most part its all the same.

That is why I recommend anyone playing this game take breaks, I myself found that after several hours it became easier to get back in once I had not played for a day. All the things you want from this game as far as exploration are there. If you want to go from world to world, you can do that, so on that part the game is very good, and if that's all you want you should be happy.

I would be remiss if I did not mention that although the exploration part of the game is well hashed out, other parts are suprisingly unfinished or lackluster. Comparing the trailers we saw of this game to the finished product, its clear what we have here is not the gameplay we were promised. There are no large space battles, no portals, no sand worlds, no sand worms, etc.

What we have is mostly an exploration game with survival aspects and ship flight. The exploration parts are great, the rest is sometimes mediocre, the invisible barrier preventing you from touching the ground in your ship is annoying.

[u]Graphics[/u]

Ok so for me this game looks amazing, but I know some people find its washed out color scheme difficult to sit through at times. I am able to play the game on max settings, if I had a complaint I feel that even on these settings it could go even higher, get even better.

I do think that the worlds they have built here are as unique as you would want from planet to planet, exception being the overly repeated usage of textures you see from time to time. The effects are what you would expect from a modern game as well, I don't think there is anything wrong with them per se, but the nature of the procedural generation tends to be noticeable and immersion breaking at times. Often during flight you see land spontaneously generate and disappear, that can be annoying, but I do not know if it could be any different based on how the game works.

Space itself looks rather dull, but space is mostly empty so I'm not sure if that's really a well thought out critique of the game. Many of the systems do have some color in the form of what i'm guessing is gas.

The planets all look great from orbit in my opinion, but I was extremely disappointed by the lack of Gas Giants in the game, and stars that are merely painted in the background, despite Sean Murray's promise they would be there. (Not the gas giants, the real stars.) I'll talk a bit about the Gas Giants further below.

[u]Soundtrack[/u]

So here the music is amazing, and fits perfectly with the design of the game. It's really the soundtrack of the universe you are exploring and is one of the game's highlights for sure.



[u]Problems, Critical Issues[/u]

So let's talk a little bit about the things I have a problem with. The invisible barrier is one, but not having gas giants, that is bad and so unrealistic it borders on criminal in a space game. I'm told that the game is about exploring worlds, you can't land your ship on a gas giant because it has no land, and the atmospheric pressures would crush your little ship. Ok that's fair, but...

Then we find ourselves entering a system with a blackhole. And of course we don't want to go near it, its a black hole. But alas the game creators have turned all black holes into space tunnels. That's right, you can instantly travel great distances by entering one. Except that's not at all how a black hole works, you are thinking of a worm hole. Black holes are stars whose gravity collapsed the star in on itself. The gravitational pull is so massive, that it will crush you to an infinitely small point, a term referred to as spaghettification. This happens when the gravity closest to the event horizon is stronger than the gravity farther away. As you get closer, the end closest will begin to stretch until you are nothing more than a noodle version of yourself. That is a black hole.

But I'm told we can't have gas giants because the atmospheric pressure inside one would crush you. Come on Hello Games, at least make sense, be consistent. If you were looking for reality this game is not that.

The game also frequently crashes for some people, has weird and often funny bugs that can be game breaking at times. But that is not a problem that cannot be patched. The real problem is the lack of content. In a universe so vast, there really is little diversity. This is a problem. Hopefully one that can be fixed as they continue to patch and add dlc to the game. We desperately want more variety, more engagement in what amounts of a game of jumping from planet to planet, that's it. There is no story, sure there are some things that are interesting, like the races, and the atlas, but its not cohesive and you can ignore it if all you want to do is explore.

So my final verdict, and I'm ignoring any bugs the game currently has is

[h1]5/10[/h1] Damn I really wanted it to be higher, and maybe with added content it will, but for right now this game is unfinished, it should have been released on Early Access to allow users to give their input and see what they were buying into. It's not a terrible game as some have suggested, its a marvel of technology that we should appreciate but right now it is lacking many features, many things that make a universe as special as it is. When you look through the hubble and see the amazing universe we live in, that was the promise of what No Man's Sky could have been, instead this feels like 10% of what we expected, even at 100% of what we paid. I still recommend this game if you know what you are getting, I do like playing, and hope for more.

[u]Background:[/u]
I didn't hear about No Man's Sky until early this year. I watched the trailers, read the info, and looked at the works of Hello Games, more specifically the people that are Hello Games. I was excited for this game. As I always do, I never anticipate games to be 100% perfect, and for good reason. A lot of development companies realease a broken game that is bearly playable and then patches it through the year. I know Hello Games has tried to be better than that. I bought this game for both PC and PS4. I've been playing the PS4 version everyday since release, and here's what I've got to say about the game.

[u]The Introduction[/u]
The game drops you on a random planet in the universe next to a crashed ship, presumably yours. There is no backstory to what you're doing there or why you crashed, at least I haven't come across one. Doesn't matter too much, as the game isn't about you life's story, It's about the Atlas and your adventure to the center of the universe where the Atlas resides, from what I've gathered thus far. So you need to fix up your ship and get moving, if you want. You don't have too, there is a choice. You can ignore the Atlas and the search for the center of the universe, or not. You can even do both, follow the Atlas' guidance, but taking you time doing so. Which leads me to gameplay.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
So, let's skip to when you have fixed all your broken tech, and are exploring. I just love it. When they said planet sized, they meant it. I walked for about 10 minutes and it seemed like I had only gone the distance of a 10 minute walk IRL. The mining materials is fun, a bit repetative, but mining is pretty much the same no matter how you look at it. Exploring the valleys, mountains, and bodies of water is exciting. The worlds are filled with so much stuff, it's incredible, that is if you are on a world that is filled with flora. Searching for all of the fauna can be a challenge, or a cake walk, depending on how densely populated the planet is. Scanning for minerals, landmarks, buildings, or knowledge stones is fun, especially the knowledge stones. Now space is interesting. The combat is a challenge at first, but you get use to it. I still have difficulty looking for planets with the map. 

[u]Graphics[/u]
As everone has been pointing out, there is a framerate issue, or there is a slight framerate issue. I'm running a single 980Ti @ 4K 60Hz, 32GB of ram, with the game on a SSD with a 6Gb/s connection. I can run the game on High graphics at 30FPS. When I do turn the character around after a scan, I'll see a bit of a framerate drop to about 20FPS when I run across a cluster of icons, but only for about a second.

Rating 7/10
Why? Because I think the game is great, that the ideas behind the game are fantastic, and that it has further potential. By no means is it perfect, it does have issues, but these issues are temporary. They can be fixed, and will be fixed. Once everything has been ironed out, I'd give it a 9/10. I haven't reached far in the game yet to know what more there is to give it that final one point, 

Good luck Hello Games, and the future that awaits, and good luck fellow space travelers in your journey.

[u]Update:[/u]
I have not played the game in quite some time, at least not since they added the ability to buy the larger ships. After having played a bit of the game again, I think that I stand by my original rating of 7/10.

There are many, many things I love about No Man's Sky. I love how vast the universe is, how you can experience something new (and sometimes very exciting) by simply going to the next planet. I love the mystery of the stories, learning about the races, and about the universe itself.  I really, really do enjoy this game...

...when it runs.

I've spent over 170 hours in No Man's Sky, and I can say with confidence that at least 150 of those hours were spent under 25fps, and at least a few of those hours were spent in loading screens, pushing through extreme stutters and lockups, and trying to figure out how to alleviate the newest memory leak with each update.  Entering a planet's atmosphere will cause the game to stutter heavily, looking in a direction with a lot of trees can freeze the game momentarily, and sometimes even loading screens can lock up.  Even closing the game is an adventure, and ever since the NEXT update (save for a stretch across two patches) the game would lock up so heavily that the only way to get my computer to unfreeze would be to reset it via the button on the case.

Just yesterday, that issue didn't exist.  The game also ran reasonably well, between 20 and 25fps, loaded and closed without issues.  Today saw a new update, but with a new update came old issues.  Right now, for all intents, the game barely runs at all.  My base is placed on a planet I picked specifically because it produced good framerate but even now that's toast.  I tried to close the game and the glorious hyper-lockup had returned...

My computer exceeds the minimum requirements for this game, and graphics settings don't change the performance at all.  At fully low settings I'll get the same results as I do on the High settings with nothing gained or lost on either end of the spectrum.  Even the game config file changes don't help at all.  I'm literally at the mercy of Hello Games and whether or not they can correct issues (and keep those issues gone) with each patch.  Just before the NEXT update the game ran the best it ever has so I'm still holding out hope, two years down the road, that I'll be able to finally enjoy this game some day.  Today is not that day, tomorrow doesn't look good either.
